title: Stock Futures Dip as Investors Digest Meta & Tesla Earnings: Live CNBC Updates
body:
U.S. equity futures opened lower on Thursday, with the S&P 500 down about two‑thirds of a percent and Nasdaq‑100 futures slipping roughly 0.8%, as investors processed mixed third‑quarter earnings from two of the market’s biggest technology players, Meta Platforms and Tesla. The pullback comes after a three‑day rally that saw the S&P 500 notch a winning streak and the Nasdaq Composite climb on the back of a surge in Tesla and SpaceX‑related stocks, but the latest results have injected a dose of caution into an otherwise upbeat market narrative.

Meta’s earnings report delivered a blend of solid revenue growth and lingering concerns over user engagement. The company posted a 12% year‑over‑year increase in advertising revenue, driven largely by higher ad prices and a modest rebound in ad spend from the United States and Europe. However, the firm’s daily active user count in the United States and Canada fell short of analyst expectations, prompting worries that the recent rollout of paid verification and the ongoing competition from short‑form video platforms could be eroding its core audience. While Meta’s earnings per share beat consensus estimates, the guidance for the next quarter hinted at a slower pace of growth, with the firm projecting a 5% to 7% increase in ad revenue versus the 9% to 11% many analysts had anticipated. The mixed signals led to a sell‑off in the stock, which fell about 4% in after‑hours trading, dragging down the broader S&P 500 futures.

Tesla’s quarterly results painted a more nuanced picture. The electric‑vehicle maker posted record deliveries, topping 435,000 units worldwide, and posted a 15% rise in revenue year‑over‑year, bolstered by higher average selling prices and expanding production capacity at its new Gigafactory in Texas. Nonetheless, the company’s profit margin narrowed as raw‑material costs and logistics expenses surged, prompting a 6% dip in the share price after the bell. Analysts also flagged a slowdown in the rollout of the Full Self‑Driving (FSD) software, which has been a key growth lever for the automaker. While the earnings beat on revenue, the cautious outlook for future margins and the lingering regulatory scrutiny over autonomous‑driving claims left investors wary.

The broader market reaction reflects the delicate balance between growth expectations and profitability concerns that have defined the tech sector this year. The S&P 500’s three‑day winning streak—fueled largely by strong performances in the communications and consumer discretionary sectors—was underpinned by optimism that the Federal Reserve’s monetary tightening cycle is nearing its end. Yet the earnings releases from Meta and Tesla underscore that even industry leaders are not immune to headwinds such as higher input costs, competitive pressure, and regulatory uncertainty. Nasdaq‑100 futures, which are heavily weighted toward technology stocks, were particularly sensitive to the earnings news, slipping nearly 1% as investors reassessed the risk‑reward profile of high‑growth names.

Market strategists caution that the near‑term volatility may be temporary, pointing to the resilience of the underlying macro backdrop. The U.S. labor market remains tight, consumer confidence is holding steady, and inflationary pressures appear to be moderating, all of which support a continued accommodative stance from policymakers. Moreover, the earnings season is still in its early stages, with several other heavyweight tech firms—such as Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon—set to report later this week. Their results could either reinforce the current cautious tone or provide a fresh catalyst for a rebound.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of U.S. equities will likely hinge on how quickly the tech giants can translate revenue growth into sustainable profitability while navigating regulatory scrutiny and shifting consumer preferences. If Meta can stabilize its user base and monetize its new verification model, and Tesla can manage cost pressures while delivering on its ambitious vehicle pipeline, the sector may regain its momentum. For now, investors appear to be adopting a wait‑and‑see approach, weighing the latest earnings data against the broader economic outlook before committing to the next leg of the market’s rally.
